nameStory: Golenkinia gets its name from Russian botanist Mikhail Golenkin, who studied microscopic algae in the early 1900s. The species name 'radiata' means 'with rays' in Latin, describing how this tiny organism looks like a spiky ball with needle-like projections radiating outward in all directions.
description: **Note: This identification is uncertain due to limited reference material.** Golenkinia radiata is a microscopic freshwater green alga that you'd need a microscope to see properly. Each individual cell is spherical and covered with long, thin spines that stick out like a sea urchin. These tiny organisms are only about 10-20 micrometers across (that's smaller than the width of a human hair), but they can sometimes form visible colonies in pond water.

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Individual cells are invisible to the naked eye - you'll need at least 400x magnification to see the distinctive spiky structure clearly

idTips.label: Spiny appearance
idTips.description: Under a microscope, each cell looks like a tiny green ball covered in long, straight spines radiating outward like pick-up sticks

idTips.label: Green coloration
idTips.description: The cell interior appears bright green due to chlorophyll, while the spines are typically colorless or pale

idTips.label: Floating habit
idTips.description: Found suspended in the water column rather than attached to surfaces, often giving pond water a slightly greenish tint when abundant

habitat: **Habitat information uncertain.** Likely found in freshwater ponds, quiet streams, and temporary pools throughout New England's lower elevations. Prefers nutrient-rich water and may be more common in areas with agricultural runoff or natural organic matter.

seasonality.spring: **Seasonal information uncertain.** Populations may begin growing as water temperatures warm and daylight increases.
seasonality.summer: Likely most abundant during warm months when conditions favor rapid algal growth and reproduction.
seasonality.fall: Populations may persist into early fall but likely decline as temperatures drop and daylight decreases.
seasonality.winter: Probably dormant or present in very low numbers during cold months, surviving as resistant spores.

funFact: Despite being practically invisible to us, these spiky microscopic spheres are actually sophisticated solar-powered factories that help produce much of the oxygen we breathe - and their needle-like spines may have inspired the design of some modern water filtration systems!
confusionNotes: **Confusion species uncertain.** Under a microscope, it might be confused with other spiny green algae, but the combination of spherical cells with long, straight radiating spines should distinguish it from most similar species.
contextualKnowledge: This is a microscopic organism that requires specialized equipment to observe and identify properly. Most nature enthusiasts won't encounter it directly, but it may contribute to the greenish color sometimes seen in pond water during algae blooms.
compareHints: **Comparison information uncertain due to limited data.** As apparently the only Golenkinia species recorded in New England, it would need to be compared with other microscopic spiny green algae in different families. The long, straight spines and spherical cell shape should help distinguish it from other microscopic freshwater algae.
